title: Problem Documentation and Imports
content: The header documents Erdős Problem #1019 on saturated planar subgraphs in dense graphs. A saturated planar graph on $n$ vertices has exactly $3n - 6$ edges (the maximum for planarity). The problem asks: does every graph with $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$ edges contain a saturated planar subgraph on more than 3 vertices? Simonovits proved yes. Imports Mathlib's `SimpleGraph`, `Subgraph`, and `Fintype` modules.

title: Edge and Vertex Count
content: Basic graph parameters: `edgeCount G` returns $|E(G)|$ via `G.edgeFinset.card`, and `vertexCount` returns $|V|$ via `Fintype.card V`. The entire problem is parametrized by these two quantities.

title: Planarity and Euler's Bound
content: `isPlanar G` asserts that $G$ can be embedded in the plane without edge crossings. Euler's formula for connected planar graphs ($v - e + f = 2$ with $f \ge 2$ for $v \ge 3$) gives the bound $|E| \le 3|V| - 6$. This is axiomatized as `planar_edge_bound`. The definition of `isPlanar` itself is left as `sorry` since topological planarity requires machinery beyond current Mathlib.

title: Saturated Planar Graph
content: `isSaturatedPlanar G` holds when $G$ is planar with $|V| \ge 3$ and exactly $3|V| - 6$ edges—the maximum possible for a planar graph. Equivalently, a saturated planar graph is a *maximal* planar graph: adding any edge would violate planarity. Every face in the planar embedding is a triangle (a *triangulation*). The smallest example is $K_3$ on 3 vertices (3 edges $= 3 \cdot 3 - 6$); the next is $K_4$ on 4 vertices (6 edges $= 3 \cdot 4 - 6$).

title: Edge Density Threshold
content: Three quantities: `turanEdges n` $= \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ (the Turán number $\text{ex}(n, K_3)$, maximum edges in a triangle-free graph), `additionalThreshold n` $= \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$ (the extra edges needed beyond Turán), and `saturatedPlanarThreshold n` = their sum. The predicate `exceedsThreshold G` requires $|E(G)| \ge \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$.

title: Triangles, $K_3$, and Turán's Theorem
content: Defines $K_3$ as `completeGraph 3` and axiomatizes that $K_3$ is saturated planar (3 edges $= 3 \cdot 3 - 6$). Turán's theorem is axiomatized: any graph with more than $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor$ edges contains a triangle. This is the baseline—Erdős #1019 asks what *additional* structure appears when we go $\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$ edges beyond Turán's threshold.
mathContext: $|E(G)| > \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor \Rightarrow K_3 \subseteq G$ (Turán 1941); $K_3$ is saturated planar since $3 = 3 \cdot 3 - 6$

title: Induced Subgraphs and Saturated Planar Containment
content: `inducedSubgraph G S` restricts $G$ to vertex set $S$, keeping all edges within $S$. `hasSaturatedPlanarSubgraph G k` checks for a saturated planar induced subgraph on $k$ vertices. `hasLargeSaturatedPlanarSubgraph G` requires $k > 3$—finding structure beyond mere triangles.
mathContext: $G[S].\text{Adj}(u,v) \iff G.\text{Adj}(u,v)$ for $u,v \in S$; want $\exists k > 3: G[S]$ saturated planar with $|S| = k$

title: Complete Graph $K_4$ as Saturated Planar
content: $K_4$ is the smallest saturated planar graph beyond $K_3$: it has 4 vertices and $\binom{4}{2} = 6 = 3 \cdot 4 - 6$ edges. Axiomatized as `K4_saturated_planar`. The theorem `K4_gives_large_saturated` shows that containing $K_4$ (as a clique on 4 vertices) implies containing a large saturated planar subgraph.
mathContext: $K_4$: $|V| = 4$, $|E| = 6 = 3(4) - 6$; $K_4$ is the unique saturated planar graph on 4 vertices

title: Cycle Plus Two Apex Vertices: $C_\ell + 2K_1$
content: `containsCyclePlus2K1 G l` checks for a cycle $C_\ell$ ($\ell \ge 3$) with two additional 'apex' vertices, each adjacent to every vertex of the cycle. This graph has $\ell + 2$ vertices and $\ell + 2\ell = 3\ell$ edges (cycle edges + apex-to-cycle edges). Since $3\ell = 3(\ell + 2) - 6$, it is saturated planar. It can be visualized as a 'wheel with two hubs'—two cones over a polygon sharing the same base.
mathContext: $C_\ell + 2K_1$: $|V| = \ell + 2$, $|E| = 3\ell = 3(\ell + 2) - 6$; two apex vertices each adjacent to all $\ell$ cycle vertices

title: Erdős's Construction: Lower Threshold Achievable
content: Erdős constructed graphs with $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$ edges that contain no saturated planar subgraph on more than 3 vertices. The construction starts from the Turán graph $T(n,2)$ (complete bipartite $K_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor, \lceil n/2 \rceil}$) and adds $\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$ edges forming a matching within one part. This creates triangles but no $K_4$ or $C_\ell + 2K_1$.
mathContext: $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$ is achievable without large saturated planar subgraphs

title: The Main Question: Erdős #1019
content: `erdos_1019_question` asks: does every graph with $|V| \ge 4$ and $|E| \ge \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$ contain a saturated planar subgraph on more than 3 vertices? This is universally quantified over all graphs and vertex types, making it a strong statement about the extremal threshold.
mathContext: $\forall G \text{ with } |V| \ge 4, |E| \ge \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor: \exists k > 3, G \text{ has saturated planar on } k \text{ vertices}$

title: Simonovits's Theorem — The Resolution
content: Simonovits proved (in his PhD thesis): if $|E(G)| \ge \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor$, then $G$ contains $K_4$ or $C_\ell + 2K_1$ for some $\ell \ge 3$. Both are saturated planar on $> 3$ vertices. The theorem `erdos_1019_solved` combines Simonovits's theorem with the two lemmas (`K4_gives_large_saturated`, `cyclePlus2K1_gives_large_saturated`) to resolve the problem: `erdos_1019_question` holds.
mathContext: $|E| \ge \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor \Rightarrow K_4 \subseteq G \text{ or } C_\ell + 2K_1 \subseteq G$ for some $\ell \ge 3$

title: Erdős Size Bound (1969)
content: A quantitative strengthening: graphs with $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + k$ edges contain saturated planar subgraphs on $\gg k/n$ vertices. The function `saturatedPlanarSize n k = k / n` gives a lower bound on the subgraph size. This shows that more extra edges force not just any large saturated planar subgraph, but a proportionally larger one.
mathContext: $|E| \ge \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + k \Rightarrow \exists S \subseteq V: |S| \ge k/n, G[S] \text{ saturated planar}$

title: Complete Bipartite Graph and Turán Connection
content: Defines `completeBipartite m n` as the graph on `Fin m ⊕ Fin n` with edges between parts. For $m, n \ge 3$, $K_{m,n}$ is planar iff $m \le 2$ or $n \le 2$ (Kuratowski). So large complete bipartite graphs are not planar, hence not saturated planar—connecting the construction to the planarity constraints.

title: Threshold Gap and Optimality
content: The theorem `threshold_gap` proves $\lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor = \lfloor n^2/4 \rfloor + \lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor + 1$ by `omega`. This shows the forcing threshold exceeds the construction threshold by exactly 1 edge—the sharpest possible gap. The combined `threshold_optimal` asserts: above the threshold, large saturated planar subgraphs exist; below, they can be avoided.
